title: Why index funds beat most stock pickers

scenes.headline: Most pros can't beat the market
scenes.narration: Here's an uncomfortable fact. Over long stretches, most professional fund managers fail to beat a plain, boring index fund. Let's look at why.

scenes.headline: What is an index fund?
scenes.narration: An index fund doesn't try to pick winners. It simply buys every company in a list, like the five hundred biggest US companies, and holds them all.
scenes.body: One purchase gives you a small slice of hundreds of businesses.

scenes.headline: Stock picking is a zero-sum game
scenes.narration: Before costs, the average investor earns the market's average return, because together investors are the market. If one picker beats it, someone else has to fall short.

scenes.headline: Fees quietly eat returns
scenes.narration: Active funds pay analysts and traders, and they pass that cost on to you every year. Index funds just follow a list, so they charge far less. A small fee gap compounds into a big difference over decades.
scenes.body: Lower costs mean more of the return stays in your pocket.

scenes.headline: Why index funds keep winning
scenes.narration: Put it together. Low fees, wide diversification, and no reliance on one manager's luck. It's not exciting, and that's the point.
items: No star manager to bet on

scenes.headline: Picking the winner in advance is hard
scenes.narration: Some managers do beat the market for a few years. But finding them before they win, and staying with them, is the hard part. Past stars often cool off.

scenes.headline: Start simple, stay consistent
scenes.narration: For most beginners, a low-cost index fund bought regularly and held for the long term is a sensible starting point. This is general education, not personal advice. Do your own research.
scenes.body: Not financial advice. Learn more before you invest.
